summary: Defines a DNS resource record type that maps domain names to NSAP addresses, the address format used by OSI networks. It works with any NSAP address format. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines a DNS record that associates a domain name with an OSI NSAP address. It also describes how to use a PTR record to find a name from an NSAP.

questions: map domain name to nsap address
how to map domain name to nsap
subtitle: How DNS records associate domain names with OSI network service access point addresses.

tldr.problem: Operators using CLNP had numeric NSAP addresses that were difficult to manage in shared name-to-address files.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an NSAP resource record for name-to-address mapping and uses PTR records under NSAP.INT for reverse lookups.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1706 is Historic, obsoletes RFC 1348 and RFC 1637, and is listed as updated by RFC 9121 in the unit metadata.

today: RFC 1706 is Historic. It obsoletes RFC 1348 and RFC 1637, and the unit metadata lists RFC 9121 as updating it.

sections.title: Why Publish NSAP Addresses in DNS
sections.content:
Some parts of the Internet used OSI's Connectionless Network Protocol (CLNP) and supporting routing protocols. Debugging CLNP connectivity became harder as networks grew because people relied on exchanged files that paired names with numeric NSAP addresses.

RFC 1706 defines DNS publication of domain-name-to-NSAP mappings for any NSAP address format. It distinguishes publication from registration: the authority defined by ISO 8348 remains responsible for registering NSAP addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS can publish the name associated with an NSAP address. The RFC does not change who registers NSAP addresses.

sections.title: NSAP Structure and the Selector
sections.content:
An NSAP is hierarchical, allowing different authorities to manage delegated parts of the address space. DNS servers are not expected to know the internal structure of every NSAP format. The RFC uses the U.S. GOSIP arrangement as an example of fields assigned by different authorities.

The final octet is the NSelector (NSel), which identifies a CLNP user. Because a system can have more than one such user, the RFC specifies that DNS-stored NSAP values use NSel=0; an application selects the value needed for a particular communication.
sections.plainLanguage: An NSAP contains fields managed under delegated authority. DNS stores it with a zero NSelector so applications can choose the CLNP user they need.

sections.title: The NSAP Resource Record
sections.content:
The NSAP record uses the mnemonic NSAP and DNS type code 22. It follows the standard resource-record structure: owner name, type, class, time to live, data length, and data. The record's class is IN, and its data contains the binary NSAP address in the form used in a CLNP address field.

In a DNS master file, the data is written as 0x followed by hexadecimal digits. Periods may be added for readability, but they are not sent in DNS packets. An NSAP record does not cause additional-section processing.
sections.plainLanguage: An NSAP record stores a domain name and the binary NSAP address associated with it. In a master file, hexadecimal digits make that address readable.

sections.title: Reverse Lookup with PTR Records
sections.content:
To find a name from an NSAP, the RFC uses the existing PTR record under the NSAP.INT domain. The lookup name is built by reversing the hexadecimal nibbles of the NSAP and using each nibble as a separate subdomain label.

The RFC recommends that user interfaces accept NSAPs in their usual written order and ignore periods entered for readability. The resolver can then construct the reverse name used for the PTR query.
sections.plainLanguage: A reverse lookup turns the NSAP's hexadecimal digits into labels in reverse order. A PTR query under NSAP.INT returns the associated name.

sections.title: Master Files and Security Note
sections.content:
The RFC shows forward NSAP records and reverse PTR records in DNS master-file examples. Dots may separate hexadecimal groups for readability, but they have no meaning in the transmitted record.

The security section states that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how to write NSAP and PTR records in master files. The RFC does not discuss security issues.
